transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-11
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Asha Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Redwood SE), Dr. Marina Lopez (BlueOak), Evan Turner (BlueOak SRE), Priya Singh (BlueOak ML), Samir Doshi (BlueOak CTO)

Summary: Quick hands-on walkthrough of Redwood Optimize's precision/quantization chooser. Focus: INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs, latency vs quality metrics, fallback behavior under load, and integration steps for BlueOak's production ML inference. Agreed to run a week-long sandbox microbench and share q-profile exports and a short fallback playbook.

Topics: q-profiles, INT8, FP8, mixed-precision, sampling for fidelity, kv cache impact, batching, canary rollouts, telemetry needed for quality regressions

[00:00] Asha: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, we'll keep this pretty pragmatic — show you the Optimize console, the quant profiles, and then run a few quick comparisons. Liam will drive the bench. Sorry, Jordan will drive the bench, Liam will handle the fallback rules.
[00:28] Marina: Great, thanks. Quick note: our primary constraint is sub-400ms p95 for short prompts, and we can't exceed a defined per-token cost mark, we have to keep costs below internal threshold. Also privacy — some payloads are PII.
[00:46] Asha: Yep, noted on the SLO and the data sensitivity. We'll talk about Private / VPC options briefly.
[01:10] Liam: Alright, I'll start screen sharing — bear with me if the console lags a bit. So this is Redwood Optimize, the q-profile section. On the left you can see existing profiles. The one we use for low-latency is called "fidelity-slim" — it's set to prefer INT8 quantization where model tolerates it.
[01:38] Evan: Quick question, when you say prefer INT8, is that per-layer or global quant? Our models use a mix of transformer and small conv blocks in the embedding stack.
[01:52] Jordan: Good point — the q-profile we generate is layer-aware. We do sensitivity per-layer and then pick a global policy but allow per-layer overrides. So you can have INT8 on attention and FP8 on feedforwards for example.
[02:18] Priya: How is sensitivity measured? Is it BLEU-like, or do you do logprob shifts?
[02:27] Liam: We use a couple of metrics: logprob drift, token level accuracy for your labeled evals, and a proprietary fidelity score that correlates to human evals. We'll share the csv.
[02:42] Samir: And this fidelity score — what's a 2% drop look like in terms of real output? We care about hallucination risk.
[02:51] Jordan: It depends on prompt. For your clinical triage prompts (they gave sample earlier), small factual errors can be high risk, so we usually keep FP8 or higher for that lane. For generic summarization, INT8 is often fine.
[03:12] Marina: That matches our thinking. Can you show latency numbers next to quality? Visual side-by-side?
[03:22] Liam: Yep, the console has this compare view. I'll load a precomputed bench — this is a 1k-sample microbench with mixed prompt lengths. On the left is per-profile p50/p95 latency, on right is fidelity delta vs fp16 baseline.
[03:45] [03:45] Screen noise / small pause
[03:55] Liam: So profile A (aggressive INT8) shows p95 around 320ms, p50 ~110ms, token cost down about 37% vs baseline. Fidelity delta: mean -3.4% on our fidelity score, but per-case variance is high. Profile B (hybrid INT8/FP8) gives p95 420ms, cost -21%, fidelity -0.9% mean.
[04:28] Evan: For our SLO sub-400ms p95, Profile A would pass but fidelity hit might be too big for triage. Profile B is borderline.
[04:42] Priya: Could you show an example of failure case where INT8 breaks?
[04:48] Liam: Sure — here's a sample prompt from your test set — I'll run it across both profiles. (short pause) Profile A output missed an entity and rewrote a medication name, Profile B preserved entities correctly. You can see the token probabilities dip earlier for Profile A.
[05:20] Marina: That's concerning for us. Is there an automated fallback? Like if top-k drops below threshold or confidence drops, switch to FP8 at runtime?
[05:32] Jordan: Yes, that's the recommended pattern. Redwood Optimize can emit per-response telemetry (fidelity/confidence hooks). The runtime can apply a quick check — if confidence<0.6 or if certain regex detects entity fuzziness, we re-run the request with a higher precision profile or bypass the cache. That's your rollback path.
[05:55] Samir: Re-running will double cost/latency for those requests though, right?
[06:01] Liam: Correct, it's expensive for those samples, but in practice only a small percent of traffic needs fallback if profiles are tuned. We saw less than 1.2% fallback in a similar healthcare POC after tuning.
[06:20] Evan: How do you instrument that? We need traces and token-level metrics to tie back to our monitoring stack.
[06:27] Jordan: We export telemetry to your datadog or prometheus endpoints — there's a webhook and a push-style exporter. We'll include example dashboards. Also each token has timing, quant-mode, and KV cache hits in traces.
[06:45] Marina: Show me the KV cache impact — we deploy many short-context prompts that benefit from prefix caching.
[06:52] Liam: Right — prefix caching reduces latency a lot for repeated context. When we use KV caching, we saw p95 drop by 30-40% for those flows. Note: caching interacts with quantization because cached KV entries are specific to a model/precision variant. If you have mixed-precision fallbacks, we either cache per-variant or invalidate on fallback. There's a tradeoff.
[07:23] Priya: So do we end up duplicating cache entries for FP8 and INT8? That could blow memory.
[07:29] Jordan: Yep that's why we often recommend sticky routing — route a given customer/route to a precision lane for a period to avoid duplicate caches, and only run the fallback re-run on mismatch. We can also use a small in-memory LRU per variant.
[07:45] [08:00] Liam: Let me switch to the lab bench. I'm going to run a small on-the-fly test — three prompt buckets: short (<=40 tokens), mid (~120 tokens), long (~450 tokens). We'll compare profile A (INT8 aggressive), profile B (hybrid), and FP16 baseline.
[08:22] [08:22] (console clicking)
[08:30] Liam: Kickoff bench... first short prompt results arriving. Profile A p50 95ms, p95 310ms; Profile B p50 130ms, p95 410ms; FP16 baseline p50 140ms, p95 460ms. Quality wise (authored label set) Profile A accuracy 91%, Profile B 96%, FP16 97.5% on this bucket.
[09:04] Marina: These numbers are helpful. Could you export the raw csv with per-sample diffs and confidence so we can run our own analysis?
[09:13] Asha: Absolutely, we'll push the csv to the sandbox and give you a link.
[09:18] Samir: On cost, our finance team wants an estimate for 10M tokens/month with 60% short prompts; can you provide a ballpark for both profiles and projected savings?
[09:30] Asha: We'll provide a pricing ballpark — the console also has a cost estimator. We'll run numbers tied to your token mix and the bench results.
[09:37] Priya: Any nuance for models with mixed RNN/transformer parts? Our inference graph has a custom embedding preprocessor.
[09:45] Jordan: Most custom preprocessing doesn't affect the quantization inside the transformer core, but warmup and batching differs. We'll ask for your actual docker image or a small replica to run locally in private mode if needed.
[09:58] Evan: Security question: how is key management done if we use Redwood Private? Our keys must never leave our KMS.
[10:05] Liam: In Private deployment we integrate with your KMS/HSM. The inference nodes never persist plaintext keys outside memory. Audit logs are available and we can show SOC2 excerpts. We'll attach the security checklist.
[10:22] Marina: Good. Back to precision: what about FP8? We heard was a middle ground — how stable is FP8 across prompt types?
[10:31] Jordan: FP8 tends to preserve logits better than INT8 in many models; in our bench FP8 hybrid preserved 0.3-1.1% fidelity delta vs fp16 while giving 18-28% cost improvement. FP8 adoption is model-dependent though; some older weights quantize poorly.
[10:50] Priya: So we'd want an automated sampling plan: run a sensitivity sweep on a representative sample, choose a hybrid profile with layer overrides, then pilot with 1% traffic, watch regressions, then ramp.
[11:05] Asha: Exactly — typical rollout recipe: 1) offline sensitivity sweep (q-profile export); 2) small sandbox bench; 3) 1% canary for production with telemetry and auto-fallback enabled; 4) ramp to desired traffic. We automate steps via the console.
[11:26] Marina: Could you show the canary controls? We need ability to route by header, user, or percentage and set thresholds for automatic rollback.
[11:36] Liam: Sure — routing policy here supports header-based routing, route-by-user-id (hashing), and percentage. You can set SLO thresholds e.g. p95 latency and fidelity delta. If thresholds pass, we continue ramp. If not, automatic rollback triggers a policy that re-routes to FP16 or hybrid.
[11:58] Evan: How long before rollback happens? Immediate after threshold breach? We need to avoid oscillation.
[12:06] Jordan: We have a cooldown and hysteresis settings. Default is 5-minute evaluation window and a 10% rollback step, with backoff. You can tune that.
[12:18] Priya: Is the telemetry granular enough to catch rare but high-severity error modes, like hallucination on hallucination-prone prompts?
[12:27] Liam: We provide per-prompt fidelity indicators and you can add custom detectors — regexes, entity mismatch checks, or human-in-the-loop flags. Those can trigger immediate re-run and an incident marker.
[12:45] Samir: Let's talk about memory and GPU utilization. If we use FP8 and INT8 homogeneously, what's impact on GPU memory and throughput?
[12:54] Jordan: INT8 reduces memory footprint significantly which increases batching and throughput. FP8 sits between FP16 and INT8. On A100-like hardware, INT8 can often double throughput depending on kernel support, FP8 gives 1.3-1.6x. But again depends on sequence length distribution.
[13:18] Evan: For large sequences our throughput wrinkles because attention grows quadratic — any tips?
[13:25] Liam: Use dynamic batching and early KV cache for repeated context. Also consider sequence bucketing in the runtime to avoid wasting compute. Optimize suggests batching windows to maximize GPU saturation without violating latency SLO.
[13:44] Marina: Show me the Optimize recommendation engine for batching and q-profile together.
[13:50] Jordan: This page suggests an autoscaling/batching configuration based on input distribution you upload. It'll propose batch_size, max_wait_ms, and a q-profile per route. We used it to reduce cost 17% in prior deployments.
[14:10] [14:10] (short pause)
[14:20] Priya: One of our concerns is model drift — after a model update how do the q-profiles carry over?
[14:28] Liam: Q-profiles are model-versioned. When you update a model, Optimize suggests a fresh sensitivity run. We keep old profiles so you can rollback. You can pin a route to a profile/model pair.
[14:44] Samir: If we use Dedicated GPUs with Redwood, do we get more predictable latency?
[14:50] Asha: Yes, Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and stricter SLOs. We can also set up burst capacity for peak windows. Private deployment adds VPC isolation.
[15:05] Evan: For our proof of concept we want to test both Hosted and Dedicated to compare. Possible?
[15:10] Jordan: Yes, we can provision a small Dedicated slice for your POC or run the bench in our hosted sandbox emulating your traffic. We'll include options in the follow-up.
[15:24] Marina: Let's talk about the human review flow — if fallback triggers are too frequent we don't want ops noise. Can we aggregate incidents and only alert on thresholded rates?
[15:34] Liam: Yep, alerts are rate-based and severity thresholds are configurable. We also include a digest of flagged responses for sampling rather than alerting on every re-run.
[15:48] Priya: A practical question: how long does a sensitivity sweep take on our ~1k sample set?
[15:55] Jordan: Typically a few hours for a full layerwise sweep on a mid-sized model; optimized passes can finish in under an hour with sampling heuristics. For the bench we ran earlier it was precomputed overnight.
[16:10] Evan: Can we run sensitivity on-prem? We may not want raw examples leaving our environment.
[16:17] Liam: Yes, we support on-prem/local runners that produce q-profiles and metrics locally and only send the profile metadata to the control plane if you choose. That aligns with Private deployment.
[16:31] Marina: For regulatory needs we need audit trails and per-call PII redaction — does the runtime support PII filters before telemetry export?
[16:39] Jordan: Yes, you can mask or hash PII before sending telemetry. You can also keep telemetry inside VPC. We'll include a section in the security checklist.
[16:54] Samir: Quick tangent — what about competitor model support? We may want to test Anthropic or other open weights.
[17:00] Asha: We support a catalog of models and can bring customer-supplied weights in Private. For hosted we have curated models; Anthropic is often a managed partner and we can run comparisons.
[17:15] Priya: Ok, can we see an automated experiment summary? Something that says 'Profile A - X% cost save, Y fidelity loss, Z fallback rate'?
[17:24] Liam: Yep — Optimize's experiment view summarizes per-profile cost delta, fidelity delta, latency buckets, and a predicted fallback rate. I'll pull up a recent example — here's a table: Profile, CostDelta, FidelityDelta, PredictedFallbackRate.
[17:44] (table shown) Profile A: -37% cost, -3.4% fidelity, 1.9% fallback; Profile B: -21% cost, -0.9% fidelity, 0.6% fallback; FP16: baseline
[18:00] Marina: That predicted fallback rate is important — how is that calculated?
[18:05] Jordan: It's based on per-sample sensitivity and a heuristic threshold for confidence; we simulate thresholds across your sample set. We'll share the sim script.
[18:16] Evan: Let's confirm action plan: we want q-profile export and sandbox access, run bench, and then meet for POC sync Oct 20.
[18:24] Asha: Noted. We'll send credentials today.
[18:30] Priya: One last technical detail — tokenization differences between our tokenizer and Redwood's runtime. We have a custom tokenizer with special clinical tokens. Any gotchas?
[18:39] Jordan: Tokenization differences can change the quant sensitivity because sequence length and token boundaries change. For sensitivity runs we prefer using your tokenizer — if you provide it we can run bench with identical tokenization. For Private, that's straightforward.
[18:58] Samir: On fallback cost modeling, can you provide an example where fallback rate 1% impacts overall cost?
[19:04] Liam: Roughly: if baseline is $X per token, 1% fallback that doubles cost for those requests adds ~1% extra to overall cost (plus overhead). We'll model exact numbers in the pricing note.
[19:20] Marina: Are there any known edge cases where INT8 has catastrophic failures?
[19:25] Jordan: Rarely — models with low-weight dynamic range or custom ops can fail. Also some sequence-to-sequence behavior like arithmetic or structured outputs can degrade. We always surface those as part of sensitivity.
[19:40] Priya: Would you recommend starting with FP8 hybrid rather than INT8 full?
[19:44] Asha: For BlueOak's clinical use case I'd recommend FP8 hybrid for most production lanes, keep INT8 for non-critical low-latency lanes, and use auto-fallback for high-risk prompts.
[19:58] Evan: Ok, what about observability costs — are logs and traces extra?
[20:04] Asha: There's an observability retention tier; low-volume telemetry included, extended retention or high-resolution traces are an add-on. We'll include options.
[20:18] Marina: Could you also show us a short run of a canary ramp? Even a simulation inside the console would help.
[20:26] Liam: Sure — I'll simulate a 1% -> 10% ramp with automated checks. (sim running) At 1% no alarms. At 5% slight fidelity regression on a narrow subset, fallback rate hits 0.8% so policy triggers a 2x cooldown and reduces to 3% while flagging samples.
[21:00] Marina: We like the sample flagging and digest feature. That helps ops triage.
[21:08] Priya: For the POC can you include one of your runbooks for rollback and an incident template?
[21:14] Jordan: Yes, we'll attach a triage playbook, the rollback policy examples, and a sample incident report.
[21:28] Evan: One more infra question: what resource limits do you recommend per pod for hybrid profiles?
[21:34] Liam: It depends on batch size and model size, but typically 40-60GB GPU memory for medium-large models with FP16; INT8 lowers it a lot — we can recommend per-model sizing once we see your model.
[21:50] Samir: For scheduling the Follow-up: Oct 20 at 1600 UTC works?
[21:57] Asha: Works for us, I'll hold the slot.
[22:02] Marina: Anything else from BlueOak side?
[22:07] Priya: No, just the action items we discussed.
[22:10] Asha: Great — quick recap: we'll send q-profile export, sandbox creds, security checklist, and pricing ballpark. Liam/Jordan will run the microbench and push csv. We'll reconvene Oct 20.
[22:27] [22:27] (small side chat)
[22:40] Transcript notes: occasional background noise; speaker overlap in a few places; some product names transcribed as "optimize console" or just "Optimize" interchangeably.

End of transcript
